articles.title: Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries – that hurts the companies, too
articles.takeaway: Physical climate risk is shaping where multinationals choose to invest. Firms that avoid climate-vulnerable countries reduce one set of exposures but may give up access to growing markets and critical minerals, so location risk needs to be assessed at site level, not country level.
articles.summary: The article, by a researcher in international business, argues that multinationals increasingly treat climate vulnerability as a location risk and are steering investment away from poorer, climate-exposed countries. The author cites several studies, including his own analysis of 159 countries, finding that more climate-vulnerable countries attract less foreign direct investment. Examples include Google's abandoned Chilean data centre after a permit was revoked over water concerns, a delayed Kenyan data centre project, flood losses that reduced shareholder value at listed firms, and factory shutdowns in Thailand in 2011. The author argues that avoidance harms poor countries by reducing jobs and technology transfer, and that it also costs companies access to resources such as Congolese cobalt and Indonesian nickel, where more risk-tolerant firms have already built strong positions. He proposes three remedies: adaptation aid, climate risk insurance from development banks, and more granular local risk data.
keyPoints: Climate vulnerability is increasingly part of the location decision for factories, mines and offices, alongside traditional political and economic risks.

Several studies find that more climate-vulnerable countries receive less foreign direct investment; the author reports a 12% fall in FDI for each one-point rise on a 100-point vulnerability scale, holding other factors constant.
Companies rarely state climate reasons for avoiding a location, but visible cases include a halted US$200 million data centre in Chile and a suspended US$1 billion Kenyan project.
One analysis of 71 large listed firms found that major flood losses were followed by an average 5% fall in shareholder value over the next year, after adjusting for market movements.

Avoidance has a cost: the Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world's cobalt and Indonesia is the dominant nickel producer, and more risk-tolerant firms have secured strong positions there.

modules.reading: In supply chain terms, the article is about disruption risk and the design of a sourcing and production network. Flooded factories in Thailand in 2011 halted car production at several major manufacturers, showing how a local shock can spread through a network. The concentration of cobalt and nickel supply in a few climate-exposed countries is a sourcing and supply-security problem. A student of this module should see the article as a case for building resilience into network design rather than simply exiting a region.

The article treats location as a strategic choice that shapes long-run competitive position. Environmental factors, one of the PESTEL dimensions, now carry investment-deciding weight. The author also suggests that risk-tolerant firms have built defensible positions in valuable mineral resources, which connects to resource-based arguments about advantage. Strategists should note that a cautious policy of avoidance is itself a strategic decision with consequences for access to markets and inputs.

From a finance perspective, the article describes climate risk as something that raises the cost of projects and makes them harder to finance. The 5% fall in shareholder value after major flood losses shows investors pricing physical risk. Insurance and development-bank risk sharing are presented as ways to reduce the risk premium that investors demand. A finance student should consider how climate exposure changes cash flows, discount rates and the value of risk transfer.

The article describes a mismatch in which climate damage falls mainly on countries that contributed little to emissions. Economists would see this as an externality that is not reflected in location and investment prices. The author's argument that aid for adaptation can attract investment is a claim about correcting an information or risk failure in the market. Students should note that this is a claim about correlation in the author's own study, and that causation needs more evidence.

applications.concept: Christopher and Peck: supply chain risk management and resilience
applications.theory: Supply chain risk arises from disruptions that can be internal or external to the network, and they can propagate through interconnected partners. Resilience is the capacity of a network to resist disruption and recover to an acceptable performance level. Firms reduce exposure by mapping vulnerabilities, improving visibility, and building redundancy or flexibility into sourcing and production.
applications.link: The 2011 Thai floods halted Toyota, Nissan and Honda production when local factories flooded, which shows how a single localised event can disrupt parts supply across a manufacturing network. The article's concentration of cobalt in the Democratic Republic of Congo and nickel in Indonesia represents a single-region dependency for critical inputs. Vietnam's infrastructure losses, estimated at about US$280 million for unreliable infrastructure, show how a disruption at the network's infrastructure layer can impose costs on firms. The author's point that avoidance is a blunt response maps onto Christopher and Peck's emphasis on understanding the specific vulnerabilities of each node rather than withdrawing from whole regions.
applications.critique: The framework is designed to manage risk within existing networks and says less about whether a firm should exit a country altogether, which is the decision the article is concerned with. Resilience measures such as buffer stocks or dual sourcing carry cost, and the article gives no evidence on whether they would be cheaper than the investment forgone.
applications.practice: A procurement or network director should map climate exposure at each critical site and tier, identify single-source dependencies in minerals and components, and compare the cost of dual sourcing or buffer stock against the value of access. Where exposure varies within a country, the firm should prefer site-level selection and mitigation over blanket exclusion.

applications.concept: Barney: the resource-based view and VRIO
applications.theory: A firm gains sustained competitive advantage when it controls resources that are valuable, rare, costly to imitate and organised to be exploited. VRIO is a diagnostic that tests each resource on these four dimensions. Advantage rests on resources that competitors cannot easily obtain or copy.
applications.link: The article reports that companies with a greater tolerance for risk have established strong positions in the Congolese cobalt and Indonesian nickel industries. Access to these minerals is valuable and rare because the supply is concentrated in a few countries. Firms that are willing to operate in climate-exposed locations hold a capability that cautious competitors lack, which makes it difficult to imitate quickly. The author's claim that cautious firms surrender access to important resources is a VRIO argument in reverse: forgoing a valuable, rare resource means forgoing a potential source of advantage.
applications.critique: VRIO is largely static and inward-looking, and it does not explicitly account for the risk that makes a resource valuable and scarce. Climate events or expropriation could erode a resource rapidly, and the article provides no data on the returns earned by risk-tolerant firms, so the advantage claim is plausible but not demonstrated.
applications.practice: A strategy team should test whether the target resource is valuable, rare, inimitable and organised after accounting for climate exposure. If it passes, the team should consider how to secure it through local partnerships, insurance-backed projects or staged investment rather than a simple accept-or-reject decision.

applications.concept: CAPM and the weighted average cost of capital (WACC)
applications.theory: The capital asset pricing model sets the required return on equity as the risk-free rate plus beta multiplied by the market risk premium. The weighted average cost of capital blends the cost of equity and debt, and it is used as the discount rate in net present value appraisal. A higher perceived risk raises the discount rate, which lowers the present value of future cash flows and can make a project unattractive.
applications.link: The article says climate risk makes projects in vulnerable countries more expensive, less attractive and harder to finance, which corresponds to a higher discount rate or risk premium on these projects. The 5% fall in shareholder value after major flood losses at 71 listed firms suggests that investors price physical climate risk in equity values. The author's proposal that development banks provide climate insurance is effectively a means of transferring part of the cash-flow risk, which would reduce the required premium and support the project's NPV.
applications.critique: CAPM beta measures systematic market risk, but climate hazards are often location-specific and may not be captured by historic market co-movement. Applying a single country risk premium to all projects treats a city site and a rural site as equally risky, which the article itself criticises. Long horizons also make historic betas and fixed discount rates unreliable.
applications.practice: An appraisal team should model climate hazards explicitly in forecast cash flows, through lower output, higher insurance and repair costs or project delay, rather than simply raising the discount rate. They should compare project NPVs with and without available insurance and use site-specific risk assessments where possible.

applications.concept: Externalities and market failure
applications.theory: A negative externality arises when an activity imposes costs on third parties that are not reflected in market prices, leading to outcomes that are inefficient from a societal perspective. Market failure means the price system does not allocate resources efficiently. Remedies include taxes, regulation, property rights or direct provision of public goods such as adaptation infrastructure.
applications.link: Climate change is a large externality: emissions from high-income countries impose costs on low- and middle-income countries, which the article notes are responsible for only a small share of emissions yet face much of the damage. Location decisions by firms do not account for these wider welfare costs, so investment flows away from the places that most need it. The author's 2025 finding that adaptation aid is associated with more FDI fits a corrective view in which public funding reduces the perceived risk that private investors would otherwise price in.
applications.critique: Externality theory assumes that costs can be measured and internalised, but climate damage is uncertain, distributed across generations and difficult to attribute to specific investment decisions. The FDI–aid link is a correlation within the author's study and may reflect other factors, such as governance quality or existing investment ties, so causal claims should be stated cautiously.
applications.practice: A policymaker or development bank should identify the adaptation infrastructure and risk-sharing instruments that would lower the expected cost of investment in exposed regions, and should target them where the benefit to local development is greatest. A firm should treat the wider cost of avoidance, including reputational and stakeholder costs, as part of its sustainability and risk assessment.

caseStudy.scenario: A diversified mining company is considering a new cobalt processing plant in a central African country that ranks highly on climate vulnerability. Its internal risk model labels the whole country as high risk, and some competitors have already invested in neighbouring sites. Local infrastructure is fragile, and the plant would need reliable power and water supplies.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on whether the company should invest in the proposed plant, and critically evaluate the conditions under which investment would be justified.
evidence: The author's analysis suggests a 12% reduction in foreign direct investment for each one-point rise in climate vulnerability on a 100-point scale, holding other factors constant.
Firms reporting major flood losses at 71 large listed companies saw an average 5% fall in shareholder value over the following year, after adjusting for market movements.
The Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world's cobalt, and more risk-tolerant firms have established strong positions in its mineral industry.

The World Bank already offers political risk coverage that has given companies confidence to invest in several African countries, and the author proposes climate risk insurance from development banks as a similar safety net.
plan: Define the decision using the VRIO test to establish whether access to cobalt processing is valuable, rare and difficult to imitate for this firm.
Apply the risk analysis from Christopher and Peck to map site-level exposures to flood, water, heat and power failure, and identify single points of failure in the proposed network.
Use CAPM and WACC logic to show how climate risk could raise the discount rate or reduce cash flows, and recalculate NPV for the project under base and adverse climate scenarios.

Assess the effect of insurance, development-bank risk sharing and adaptation investment on the NPV and on the risk profile, and consider whether the national risk score overstates the site-level risk.
Use the externalities argument to note the wider social and reputational consequences of exit, and weigh these against the financial case.

Recommend conditional investment: proceed only at a site that passes the local risk assessment, with insurance and adaptation measures in place, and with a defined review trigger if climate exposure changes.
pitfalls: Treating the author's 12% figure or the FDI–aid association as established causal effects rather than findings from a specific study and sample.
Assessing the investment using only the national risk score, which the article itself criticises as too coarse for site-level decisions.

alsoConsider: Kraljic's purchasing portfolio matrix, to classify critical mineral inputs by supply risk and profit impact
Dunning's eclectic (OLI) paradigm, to explain location choice for foreign direct investment
Elkington's triple bottom line, to assess social and environmental consequences alongside financial return

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether a multinational's decision to avoid investing in climate-vulnerable countries is a sound strategic response to risk, and assess the alternatives available to the firm.
outline: Define climate vulnerability as a location risk and explain how it affects investment appraisal, using evidence such as the reported FDI reduction and the shareholder value effect.
Assess the strategic costs of avoidance, drawing on resource-based arguments about access to cobalt and nickel and the growth opportunities in these markets.
Evaluate alternative responses, including site-level selection, insurance, development-bank risk sharing and adaptation aid, and recommend a course of action with clear limitations.

articles.title: Which ESG disclosures link words to action?
articles.takeaway: Not all ESG narratives are equally informative. Emphasis on sustainable value chains and renewable energy tracked better environmental performance, while frequent talk about greenhouse-gas emissions and electric vehicles showed no significant link. Judge ESG reports by which topics they stress and whether those topics connect to measurable outcomes, not by their volume.
articles.summary: Savin, López Carel and Schlindwein analysed 1,477 ESG reports from STOXX Europe 600 companies (2010 to 2023), using computational linguistics to identify the environmental themes firms emphasise. They tested these themes against independently measured KPIs such as emissions, energy use and environmental innovation. Only some themes, notably sustainable value chains and renewable energy, were consistently linked to stronger environmental performance. The author argues that the question should shift from whether ESG reports can be trusted as a whole to which parts of them carry real information, and that absence of a measurable link should not be read automatically as greenwashing.
keyPoints: Greater emphasis on sustainable value chains and on renewable energy was associated with better environmental outcomes.
Frequent discussion of greenhouse-gas emissions and electric vehicles showed no statistically significant relationship with environmental performance.
Across 34 topics, governance received the most attention, and environmental topics made up almost one-fifth of report content.
Discussion of emissions, electric vehicles, renewable energy and environmental subsidies rose over time.
The author suggests topics tied to operational decisions produce measurable outcomes sooner, while emissions strategies may take longer or be poorly captured by current indicators.

modules.reading: The article is about sustainability reporting, a core concern of supply chain sustainability. Its strongest finding concerns sustainable value chains and renewable energy, which are supply-side, operational decisions with measurable effects. A supply chain student should see this as evidence that the environmental impact of a firm lies largely in how its chain is designed and run, and that reporting on those areas is more informative than generic commitments. It also shows why sustainability must be measured across more than one dimension.

For a finance student the article concerns how investors and rating agencies read non-financial information. The author argues that counting disclosures or relying on aggregate ESG scores is inadequate, and that investors need to distinguish topics by their informational value. This connects to information asymmetry between managers and capital providers, and to the reliability of disclosure as a basis for valuation and risk assessment. Students should consider how ESG signals enter cost of capital and risk judgements.

The article examines the gap between what companies say about environmental priorities and what they achieve. In strategic planning terms, ESG reports are statements of intended strategy, while KPIs approximate realised strategy. The finding that some stated priorities track outcomes and others do not invites analysis of where intentions and results diverge, and why. Students should consider whether reporting is a communication exercise or a tool for demonstrating how priorities translate into action.

applications.concept: Triple bottom line (Elkington)
applications.theory: The triple bottom line holds that organisational performance should be assessed across economic, social and environmental dimensions together, sometimes called people, planet and profit. Each dimension should be measured and reported so that trade-offs are visible. It is widely used to frame sustainability reporting and supply chain responsibility.
applications.link: The article's strongest result concerns sustainable value chains, which relate to the environmental and supply-side dimension of the triple bottom line and are tied to operational decisions. Renewable energy deployment also produced measurable outcomes linked to environmental performance. By contrast, emissions and electric vehicle narratives, although frequently discussed, showed no significant link with the KPIs used. This suggests the environmental dimension is not uniformly reported, and that breadth of coverage across the triple bottom line does not guarantee that each dimension reflects performance.
applications.critique: The triple bottom line is a framing device rather than a measurement method, and it does not say how to weight the three dimensions when they conflict. Its breadth may encourage firms to report widely without showing which environmental claims are substantive, which is the problem the article identifies.
applications.practice: A supply chain manager applying this framework should report environmental performance using measurable indicators tied to specific operational levers, such as supplier sustainability, energy sourcing and logistics emissions. Disclosures on each dimension should be linked to the KPIs they claim to influence, with trade-offs stated explicitly.

applications.concept: Deliberate and emergent strategy (Mintzberg)
applications.theory: Mintzberg distinguishes deliberate strategy, the intentions an organisation sets out, from realised strategy, what actually happens. The gap between them comes from unrealised intentions and from emergent strategies that arise from learning and circumstances. Managers should monitor realisation rather than assume intentions have been carried out.
applications.link: ESG reports function as public statements of intended strategy, and the KPIs for emissions, energy use and environmental innovation approximate realised strategy. The article finds that emphasis on some themes, such as sustainable value chains and renewable energy, aligns with better outcomes, while emphasis on emissions and electric vehicles does not show a consistent link. This pattern is consistent with a gap between intended and realised strategy in some areas. The author also notes that some initiatives take years to show effects, which means the gap may partly be a timing issue.
applications.critique: Mintzberg's distinction assumes realised strategy is observable in clear actions. For environmental initiatives, lags and imperfect indicators mean a missing statistical link may reflect measurement limits rather than unrealised intentions. The article warns against reading non-significance as greenwashing for this reason.
applications.practice: A strategy team should set measurable milestones for each stated environmental priority and track them against KPIs over time. Where realised outcomes lag, the team should explain the reasons and revise intentions openly, rather than expanding narrative coverage.

applications.concept: Agency theory (principal-agent problem)
applications.theory: Agency theory, associated with Jensen and Meckling, holds that shareholders (principals) delegate decisions to managers (agents) whose interests and information may differ. Information asymmetry creates monitoring problems and agency costs, which disclosure and independent verification can reduce. Investors seek reliable signals of managerial effort and performance.
applications.link: Investors cannot directly observe a firm's environmental effort, so they rely on ESG reports as a monitoring channel. The article shows that the informational value of these reports varies by topic, so volume and aggregate scores are poor guides. Investors who weigh disclosures about sustainable value chains and renewable energy more heavily, and discount unsupported claims on emissions, would be using disclosure as a more effective monitoring tool, in line with the article's advice to distinguish topics.
applications.critique: Agency theory assumes managers may act opportunistically, but the firm controls what it discloses, so ESG reports are themselves a managerial choice and an endogenous signal. The theory does not explain why firms emphasise weakly informative topics, which may reflect legitimacy concerns rather than agency problems.
applications.practice: An investor applying this framework should map each ESG claim to a measurable KPI and give more weight to topics with demonstrated links to performance. Engagement with the company should ask for independent verification and time-bound targets for the topics that matter most.

caseStudy.scenario: A large listed manufacturer publishes a detailed ESG report that dedicates many pages to governance and to its plans for emissions reduction and fleet electrification. Its report says much less about how it manages sustainability across its supplier network and its energy sourcing. An institutional investor is considering whether to increase its holding and wants to know which parts of the report can be relied on as evidence of environmental progress.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate whether the company's ESG report provides reliable evidence of its environmental performance, and advise the investor on how to use the report in its decision.
evidence: The study analysed 1,477 ESG reports from STOXX Europe 600 companies published between 2010 and 2023.
Sustainable value chains and renewable energy were consistently associated with better environmental performance.
Greenhouse-gas emissions and electric vehicles showed no statistically significant relationship with environmental performance.
Governance received the most attention across the 34 topics identified, while environmental topics made up almost one-fifth of report content.
plan: Define the problem using the article: volume of disclosure does not equal informativeness, and the question is which topics carry information.
Apply the distinction between intended and realised strategy (Mintzberg) to compare the report's stated priorities with what can be measured.
Use the finding on sustainable value chains and renewable energy to identify which claims are most credible and which should be verified.
Apply agency theory to explain why the investor faces an information asymmetry and why independent verification matters.
Note the article's caution that the absence of a measurable link does not prove greenwashing, and that lags may explain it.
Recommend a decision: weight supply-side and renewable energy disclosures, request evidence and time-bound targets for emissions claims, and engage the company before changing the holding.
pitfalls: Treating the absence of a significant link for emissions as proof that the company is greenwashing, which the article explicitly cautions against.
Assuming that the most detailed or longest report is the most informative, when the article's central point is that topic matters more than volume.

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether corporate sustainability reporting provides reliable evidence of environmental performance, and discuss how supply chain managers and investors should use such reports to assess progress.
outline: Explain the distinction between the volume of ESG disclosure and its informational value, using the article's evidence on which topics are linked to measured outcomes.
Apply the triple bottom line and the intended-versus-realised strategy distinction to explain why some environmental narratives track performance and others do not, including the role of time lags.

Critically evaluate the limits of the evidence, including correlation rather than causation, imperfect KPIs and the risk of misreading absent links, then recommend how managers and investors should respond.

articles.title: More work than it looks: the new jobs coming from AI adoption
articles.takeaway: The jobs question for AI depends less on the technology than on whether organisations and workers can build the 'missing middle' of facilitators who redesign work around AI, so the policy task is to create routes into those roles.
articles.summary: Teather argues that the workforce is shaping AI adoption, not just adapting to it. Using the history of the synthesiser, electricity in car manufacturing and personal computers, he claims that gains come from redesigning work around a new technology, which needs engineering and organisational skill, rather than from simply using it. He introduces the AI Labor Stack, with innovators, users and facilitators as its three layers. In a study of about 94,000 AI-related postings at S&P 500 firms, facilitators made up roughly 60 to 80 per cent of demand, split into technical, social and infrastructural types. He ends with a policy agenda: better regional evidence, modular employer-shaped training, institutions that link universities and employers, and support for displaced workers. The argument is persuasive but rests on job adverts rather than hires, on large US firms, and on historical analogies, so it should be treated as evidence of demand rather than proof of outcomes.
keyPoints: Loss aversion makes people better at naming the jobs AI could destroy than at picturing the new jobs it could create, and the article uses this bias to frame the debate.

The article's historical case rests on a distinction: Ford's moving assembly line redesigned production around electric power, while earlier factories only used electricity for lighting, which extended hours but left work unchanged.

The AI Labor Stack divides the AI workforce into innovators who build frontier systems, users who apply them, and facilitators who deploy, integrate and govern them, and the facilitators are the focus of the research.

Of about 94,000 AI-related postings at S&P 500 firms, facilitators were roughly 60 to 80 per cent, and among facilitator postings 39 per cent were purely technical, 32 per cent mixed technical and social, and nearly 20 per cent purely social.

Positive signals cited include an 81 per cent self-reported time saving among workers using generative AI, a 23 per cent advertised wage premium for AI skills in Britain, and stronger headcount growth at heavy AI adopters, though the article admits that correlation and adverts do not establish causa

modules.reading: The article is about how work is designed and who does it when a new technology arrives. The Ford example shows that tasks, roles and sequences of work had to be restructured, not just equipped with new tools, and the facilitators the author describes are people whose jobs combine technical work with redesigning processes and building trust. For a student of people, work and organisations this raises questions about job design, skill requirements, the psychological effects of new roles, and how displaced workers are supported through change.

From an operations viewpoint the article is about process redesign enabled by technology. The move from stationary car assembly to a moving line changed the process type and the economics of manufacturing, and the author's facilitators are described as adapting factory processes and redesigning workflows. Operations students should note that the article treats AI as a process and capability question rather than a product question, and that the bottleneck to adoption is the organisation's ability to change how work flows.

The article makes labour-market claims: demand for AI facilitators is substantial, advertised wages for AI skills carry a premium, and the benefits may not flow to those who currently lose work. An economics student would read this through the supply and demand for skills, the scarcity signal given by wage premiums, and the case for public intervention where training benefits spill over to other firms and workers. The evidence is thin, drawn from adverts and one survey, so the economic claims need careful testing.

For strategic planning the article is about how firms build the capacity to adopt and scale a new technology. The claim that heavy AI adopters are also growing headcount suggests that adoption is linked to growth ambitions, and facilitators can be seen as the human resources that let a firm sense opportunities and reconfigure its processes. A strategy student should treat the causal claim with caution while noting the capability argument.

applications.concept: Job Characteristics Model (Hackman and Oldham)
applications.theory: The model holds that five core job dimensions (skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy and feedback) shape three critical psychological states (experienced meaningfulness, responsibility for outcomes and knowledge of results). Those states in turn drive motivation, performance and satisfaction, with the effect moderated by employees' growth-need strength. Redesigning jobs along these dimensions is therefore a route to better work, not only a route to higher output.
applications.link: The article argues that the Ford gains came from redesigning work around electric power, with components moving through an organised sequence of tasks, while the Ceirano workshops that simply added light bulbs changed nothing about how work was done. This maps onto the model's insistence that the job itself must change, not just the tools. The facilitator roles described, especially the combined technical and social postings that make up 32 per cent of facilitator adverts, look like jobs with high skill variety and task significance, since they link AI systems to real processes and to the people who must trust them. The advice to pair technical and social responsibilities therefore fits the model's logic.
applications.critique: The model was developed for individual jobs and assumes that growth-need strength is a stable personal trait, which does not address the collective and institutional issues the article stresses, such as regional labour markets and displacement. It also cannot show whether AI-assisted users, who may be left doing narrower tasks, end up with lower skill variety, which is a risk the article does not discuss.
applications.practice: A manager introducing AI into a team should audit each affected role against the five core dimensions before rollout, identify where tasks are being narrowed and where they can be enriched, and build feedback loops from the tool into the worker's view of results. Where roles combine technical and social work, the manager should check that the people in them have the autonomy to make decisions about the AI's use.

applications.concept: Product-process matrix (Hayes and Wheelwright)
applications.theory: The matrix links the type of product, from unique custom items to standard high-volume ones, with the type of process, from jumbled job-shop flow to continuous or line flow. Consistency along the diagonal is expected, and firms that drift away from it typically face higher costs or poorer responsiveness. Changes in technology can shift which process type is viable for a given product mix.
applications.link: The Ford case in the article describes a shift from fixed-position assembly to a moving line, which moved production towards the line-flow end of the matrix, a shift made possible by electric motors that powered conveyors and tools. The article's claim that the gain came from redesigning work around the technology, rather than adding it to existing methods, is the same point the matrix makes about aligning process with product. The facilitators who adapt factory processes and redesign workflows are the people who would move an operation to a new position on the matrix.
applications.critique: The matrix was built for physical production and treats process choice as a question of layout and volume, whereas AI adoption mostly changes information flows and knowledge work, where the matrix offers little guidance. It is also static, while the article suggests that the transition could be unusually fast and that the gains may be concentrated in a few firms.
applications.practice: An operations manager should map the current product mix and volumes against the process type, then identify where AI is changing the process and whether it will push the operation off the diagonal. Staffing the transition with facilitators who understand both the process and the technology reduces the risk that new tools are bolted onto old flows.

applications.concept: Externalities and market failure
applications.theory: When an activity imposes benefits or costs on third parties that are not reflected in market prices, the market produces too little of a good with positive externalities and too much of one with negative externalities. Training is a common example of a positive externality, because some of its benefits spill over to other employers when workers move between firms, so individual firms may underinvest. Policy responses include subsidies, co-funded apprenticeships or direct public provision.
applications.link: The article's policy agenda, which calls for modular training shaped by employers, apprenticeships such as Singapore's and Ireland's, and support for smaller firms through Germany's Mittelstand-Digital, can be read as an attempt to correct an underinvestment in facilitator skills. The point that the skills are needed across sectors and regions, and that the people who gain may not be those who lose, suggests that the private returns to training fall short of the social returns. The 23 per cent advertised wage premium for AI skills signals that the skills are scarce, which is the price signal a market would normally use to draw in training.
applications.critique: The wage premium may itself be enough to attract private training without intervention, and firms may capture much of the return through retention, so the externality argument is contestable. The article provides no evidence of how much training is actually under-provided, and its evidence is adverts rather than training outcomes.
applications.practice: A policymaker applying this theory should estimate the spillover benefit of facilitator training by sector and region, then co-fund employer-led apprenticeships where the gap is largest. An employer should track how long trained staff stay, since retention determines whether it captures enough of the return to justify investing in training.

applications.concept: Dynamic capabilities (Teece)
applications.theory: Dynamic capabilities are a firm's ability to sense opportunities and threats, to seize them by committing resources to new business models or products, and to reconfigure assets, processes and structures as conditions change. They rest on managerial and organisational routines rather than on static resources, and they are the source of sustained advantage in fast-changing environments.
applications.link: The article's claim that the companies investing most heavily in AI are also reporting stronger headcount growth fits the seizing element of the theory, since adoption is linked to scaling ambition. The argument that gains depend on redesigning workflows and governing AI responsibly corresponds to reconfiguring, and the three types of facilitator map onto the capabilities a firm needs to convert a technology into advantage. The framing that the workforce drives adoption rather than merely responding to it also suggests that the human capability sits at the centre of the theory.
applications.critique: Dynamic capabilities can be hard to define and measure, and the Ramp correlation may reflect firm size, prior growth or reverse causality rather than AI adoption driving headcount. The article does not show that facilitator hiring produces the reconfiguration the theory requires, so the causal chain remains untested.
applications.practice: A strategy team should identify which routines in the business need reconfiguring to use AI, then hire or develop people for the sensing and reconfiguring roles. They should measure outcomes such as cycle time and redeployment of staff rather than counting AI spend or tool licences.

caseStudy.scenario: A mid-sized engineering manufacturer has rolled out generative AI tools across its design and planning teams, and most staff use them mainly to draft documents and search for information. The board wants to reduce headcount to cut costs, while a regional rival is recruiting people who connect AI tools to production systems and redesign its workflows. Local universities offer short AI courses, but employers say graduates have little practical experience of deploying such tools.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on how the firm should use AI adoption to create and retain work, and critically evaluate whether workforce policy or organisational redesign should take priority.
evidence: Around 81 per cent of workers who used generative AI at work said it saved them time, which shows the gain exists but does not show that it has been turned into redesigned work.
Facilitators accounted for roughly 60 to 80 per cent of AI-related job postings across sectors in the study of about 94,000 S&P 500 postings, with manufacturing among the strongest areas of demand.
A 23 per cent advertised wage premium for AI skills in British job vacancies points to scarcity of the skills needed to connect AI to real processes.
Ford's moving assembly line transformed manufacturing because the work was redesigned around electric power, while the Ceirano workshops that used electricity only for lighting left work unchanged.
plan: Define the three layers of the AI Labor Stack and locate the firm's staff within them, noting that most current use resembles the Ceirano use of a new tool without changing the work.

Apply the Job Characteristics Model to the design and planning roles to show where redesign would enrich tasks and where it would narrow them, and so where the board's headcount plan could damage motivation.
Use the product-process matrix to assess whether the firm's manufacturing process needs to shift position as AI is integrated, and therefore which facilitator skills it needs.

Apply externalities to the training question: the firm's investment in facilitator skills will benefit competitors and the local labour market, so the case for co-funded training with local universities is stronger than the firm's private return alone suggests.

Evaluate the trade-off between cost reduction and capability building using dynamic capabilities, concluding that the firm should prioritise organisational redesign and retain staff as facilitators, with workforce policy as a support, and recommend specific measures.
pitfalls: Treating job adverts as evidence of hires, or the US sample as representative of a British manufacturer's labour market, without noting the limitation.
Presenting the Ford example as proof that AI will create jobs in the same way, rather than as an analogy that depends on the redesign of work.

exam.question: Critically evaluate the argument that the benefits of AI adoption depend more on the redesign of work and the availability of facilitator skills than on the technology itself.
outline: Define the missing middle and facilitators, using the AI Labor Stack and the evidence on posting shares, and explain why the author sees them as central to adoption.
Contrast technology-led and organisation-led adoption using the Ford and Ceirano examples and the personal computer analogy, and assess how far the historical comparison supports the argument.
Evaluate the evidence and the policy implications, noting the limits of adverts and the US sample, the risk of displacement, and the case for employer-shaped training and institutions.

articles.title: Lessons From Tech’s Diversity Disclosures
articles.takeaway: Publishing diversity data before building the people, budgets and authority to deliver on it invites backlash and, when the climate shifts, retreat. Durable change depends on operational capacity and internal political support, not on disclosure alone.
articles.summary: The article traces how Jesse Jackson pressed Silicon Valley to publish workforce demographic data, beginning with Google's 2014 disclosure, after which reporting became the norm within about a year. Its central argument is that transparency raised visibility faster than companies built the capacity to act, so when lawsuits and political shifts changed the risk calculus, firms retreated and stand-alone reports largely disappeared. The author argues that lasting progress depends on quieter, high-capacity programmes such as recruitment pipelines and mentoring, protected by an internal coalition, and recommends keeping those running while shielding them from public scrutiny until the climate improves.
keyPoints: Jackson's 2014 campaign relied on a concrete, data-based demand rather than moral appeals, and won its first concession through a private understanding with Google's chief legal officer before the shareholder meeting.

Google's first release showed very low representation of Black, Hispanic and female employees, particularly in engineering. Its move made disclosure look like leadership, and other firms followed within weeks.
The article claims investors repriced companies by more than a billion dollars once gender diversity data emerged, though it presents this as limited to gender rather than race.

The author separates visibility from capacity. Reports record static snapshots and omit the operational machinery of hiring, promotion, mentoring and accountability. High visibility with low capacity is the danger zone.

By the article's account, 24 of 25 targeted firms initially complied, but a decade later only one still publishes a stand-alone report, about a dozen fold figures into ESG or annual filings, and eleven have stopped reporting.

modules.reading: This is a case about organisational change, culture and HR practice, and the gap between what an organisation says and what its systems actually do. The article treats diversity programmes as change initiatives facing resistance from both sides, and separates the visible artefact (the report) from the under-resourced machinery of hiring and promotion. A PWO student should see it as an example of why commitments made without changed routines and assumptions do not last.

The article is about power, influence and coalition-building in leading change. Jackson's success depended on relationships with a senior insider, and the author argues that programmes survive only when insiders form a coalition and protect resources. It also raises ethical questions about leaders choosing between accountability and strategic silence, which a leadership student should evaluate.

The article is about how external political and legal conditions shape corporate choices about disclosure. Lawsuits, elections, quota law and federal reporting rules change the risk calculus, and the author describes firms responding by going quiet rather than adapting openly. A strategy student should treat this as an environmental analysis problem and ask how firms should plan for political cycles.

applications.concept: Lewin's three-step change model and force field analysis
applications.theory: Kurt Lewin proposed that change involves unfreezing an existing equilibrium, moving to a new state, and refreezing it so the new behaviour becomes routine. The equilibrium is a balance between driving forces that push for change and restraining forces that resist it. Change succeeds when driving forces are strengthened or restraining forces weakened, and the new state must be anchored to last.
applications.link: Jackson's campaign acted as a driving force that unfroze the old norm of secrecy, and investor reaction and press impatience added pressure. The 'trade secret' culture and legal caution were restraining forces, which Google's concession and the argument that rivals should follow its lead weakened. By 2015 disclosure had become the rule, which looks like refreezing, but the later reversals driven by lawsuits and elections show that restraining forces returned. The article's point that reports omit the operational machinery suggests the new state was anchored at the level of reporting rather than in hiring and promotion practice.
applications.critique: Lewin's model assumes a reasonably stable new equilibrium that managers can plan, whereas the article describes an externally driven and cyclical environment in which restraining forces keep returning. The refreezing stage is therefore the weak point, and it needs to be built into routine systems rather than public documents.
applications.practice: A manager would map the driving and restraining forces around any programme, separating internal from external ones, and strengthen internal drivers such as protected budgets and named owners before making a public commitment. Refreezing should be built into hiring and promotion processes so the change can survive a shift in external pressure.

applications.concept: Schein's three levels of organisational culture
applications.theory: Edgar Schein described culture in three levels: visible artefacts (what can be seen and heard), espoused values (the stated goals and strategies), and basic underlying assumptions (taken-for-granted beliefs that actually guide behaviour). When espoused values run ahead of underlying assumptions, artefacts can be produced without changing what people believe or do, and the culture becomes unstable.
applications.link: Diversity reports are artefacts and espoused values. They are highly visible, easy to publish once Legal approves, and signal commitment. The article's point that a report omits the machinery of recruitment, promotion and mentoring implies that underlying assumptions about who is hired and advanced were not altered. The author notes that diversity offices were visible but under-resourced, and that hiring was treated as the existential bottleneck so that HR meant recruiting. This is the mismatch Schein's levels would predict when stated values outpace assumptions and resources.
applications.critique: Schein's model is descriptive and gives little practical guidance on how to move from artefacts to assumptions. The article's own prescription of quiet, protected programmes implicitly accepts that visible commitments and operating reality can diverge for long periods without resolution.
applications.practice: A manager should audit the gap between what is published and what is practised, checking whether hiring and promotion decisions, budgets and outcome accountability match stated goals. Investment should go first into the systems and people that embody the assumptions, with public communication following once the practice exists.

applications.concept: French and Raven's bases of power
applications.theory: John French and Bertram Raven identified five bases of social power: reward, coercive, legitimate, expert and referent power. A leader's influence depends on which of these bases they can draw on and on whether others accept their authority as legitimate. Leaders pursuing difficult change usually combine several bases, because formal authority alone is often insufficient.
applications.link: The article's account of the first concession depends on relationships. Jackson's private understanding with Google's chief legal officer, the company's only senior Black executive at the time, made a public reversal possible, and that executive's standing gave him expert and legitimate power to sell a controversial idea internally. Jackson's referent power among civil rights allies created external pressure. The author also argues that Legal's assessment of litigation risk can stop disclosure, which shows how the legitimate power of another function can block change. Later, the article says controversial programmes survive only when insiders form a coalition, which pools influence across these bases.
applications.critique: The framework describes sources of power but not how to sustain them over time. The article's evidence is largely anecdotal and drawn from one campaign's perspective, so a student should be careful about attributing the shift to personal relationships alone rather than to reputational and investor pressure.
applications.practice: A leader pursuing a difficult change should identify who holds legitimate, expert and referent power in the organisation and build relationships with them before making a public demand. They should also ensure the programme has a sponsor with formal authority and budget, so that progress does not depend on a single relationship.

applications.concept: PESTEL analysis
applications.theory: PESTEL is an environmental scanning framework that groups external factors into political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal categories. Its purpose is to identify forces that create opportunities and threats so that they can inform strategic choices. A good analysis assesses both how likely each factor is to change and how much impact it would have.
applications.link: The article identifies political and legal factors as decisive. Lawsuits and elections changed the risk calculus, the conservative movement against woke corporations shifted pressure, and U.S. law restricts quotas outside court-ordered remedies, which made goals and timetables risky. Federal EEO-1 filing duties shape what data exists even though the government does not publish it. Social factors such as press pressure and investor reaction also drove the original disclosure wave. The article shows the same external environment prompting disclosure at one point and silence at another.
applications.critique: PESTEL identifies the factors but does not say how firms should respond or who should act. The article suggests the response is deliberately concealed and political, which a static scan does not capture, and it describes an environment that swings in cycles rather than one that can be snapshotted.
applications.practice: A strategist would list the legal and political factors relevant to any public commitment, assess their likelihood and impact, and set triggers for reviewing the commitment. The response, including whether to change what is reported as well as whether to keep programmes running, should be decided in advance rather than reactively.

caseStudy.scenario: A large software company, under pressure from campaigners and investors, publishes its first workforce diversity report, showing under-representation in engineering. Two years later the figures have been folded into a general sustainability section, and a new legal challenge has made senior managers cautious about public targets. The diversity office is under-resourced, and recruitment and mentoring programmes depend on a few enthusiastic champions.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on whether the company should continue publishing workforce diversity data, and on what it should do to make any diversity commitment last through a change in the political and legal climate. Critically evaluate the view that transparency is sufficient to drive lasting change.
evidence: Of the 25 companies targeted by the 2014 campaign, 24 initially complied, but a decade later only one still publishes a stand-alone diversity report, about a dozen fold figures into ESG or annual filings, and eleven have stopped reporting.
Google's first release showed a US workforce that was 60% White, and an engineering corps with just 17% women of any race.
Google and Microsoft skipped a 2025 report after a decade of reporting, and Meta shut its Meta University recruitment programme in 2025.
The article reports that investors marked companies up or down by more than a billion dollars once gender diversity data became known.
plan: Define the problem using the article's visibility-capacity framework, explaining why high visibility with low capacity leaves the company exposed to scrutiny before it can deliver.
Apply Lewin's force field analysis to list driving and restraining forces, separating internal drivers from external pressures such as litigation, elections, investors and the press.
Use Schein's levels of culture to test whether the reports reflect changed underlying assumptions about hiring and promotion, or only artefacts and espoused values.
Use French and Raven's bases of power and stakeholder analysis to identify who can protect or obstruct programmes, and whether a sponsor with formal authority and budget exists.

Weigh the ethical and legal costs of reducing public disclosure against accountability to employees, investors and the public, and critically evaluate the article's recommendation to camouflage programmes.

Recommend that the board disclose only where it is legally and ethically defensible, fund evidence-backed programmes with named ownership, make public commitments only once capacity exists, and set review triggers for changes in the legal and political climate.
pitfalls: Presenting the article's visibility-capacity matrix as an established theory rather than the author's own analytical framework, and failing to note that its evidence is largely anecdotal.

Recommending concealment without weighing the trust and accountability costs to employees and investors, or ignoring the legal duties and constraints, such as EEO-1 filing and quota law, that bound the choice.

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether public disclosure of workforce diversity data can deliver lasting organisational change, drawing on change management and stakeholder theory.
outline: Explain the gap between visibility and capacity, using Lewin's force field analysis and Schein's levels of culture to show why visible commitments can outrun operational change.
Assess the role of power and coalitions in sustaining programmes through political cycles, using French and Raven's bases of power and stakeholder analysis.
Critically evaluate the article's recommendation to camouflage effective programmes, weighing strategic resilience against accountability and ethical costs.

articles.title: The market and social price of CEO indiscretions go beyond Jensen Huang and Nvidia
articles.takeaway: A chief executive's personal conduct is a governance and trust issue whose costs reach employees, customers and users of shared infrastructure, not just shareholders, so boards need oversight and succession plans that do not rest on one celebrated leader.
articles.summary: The author argues that Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive of Nvidia, after admitted personal misconduct with a Chinese customer and investigations into an alleged link to Chinese intelligence, matters well beyond the company's shareholders. The piece separates admitted conduct from unproven allegations, noting that the board said on 8 November it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Markets do react to CEO indiscretions: one 2018 study is cited as finding immediate shareholder losses of around 4 per cent, with links to lost customers and joint ventures, though the author warns that historical averages cannot predict this episode's losses. Exceptional performance can weaken oversight by making a celebrated leader hard to challenge, and a 2025 study comparing personal and financial misconduct is cited to argue that boards should respond according to misconduct type and firm performance. Employees, families and society bear costs that share prices do not record. Because Nvidia's hardware and software underpin AI research and commercial development, leadership turmoil could in principle disrupt downstream users, though the article presents this as a plausible channel rather than a demonstrated effect. The author recommends credible succession plans, independent investigations, enforceable conflict disclosures, protected reportin
keyPoints: Huang's resignation followed admitted personal misconduct; investigations into an alleged intelligence link were still open, and the author stresses that admitted conduct is not proof of espionage.
Nvidia named its finance chief, Colette Kress, as interim chief executive when the resignation was announced on 12 November.
A 2018 study cited in the article reports immediate shareholder losses of around 4 per cent after CEO indiscretions, with links to lost customers and joint ventures.
The article argues that exceptional performance can make challenge harder, since directors, employees and investors become dependent on a celebrated leader.
A 2025 study compares 59 personal misconduct events with 324 financial misconduct events, supporting the view that boards should respond by misconduct type and firm performance.

modules.reading: This is a case about the ethics and responsibility of a leader whose public message on character conflicts with his private conduct, and about how a celebrated leader can make challenge harder. A leadership student should read it as a test of whether influence built on personal reputation survives when that reputation is damaged. It also shows why boards and staff need legitimate ways to challenge leaders, since dependence on one admired figure weakens scrutiny. The author's careful separation of admitted conduct from unproven allegations is itself a lesson in fair judgement.

The article describes owners delegating to a chief executive whose conduct they cannot fully observe, so the economic question is how boards monitor and discipline an agent. Share price movements are the mechanism by which investors react, and the cited 4 per cent loss shows how the market prices this risk. The author also describes externalities: costs fall on employees, families and users of AI infrastructure who had no part in the decision and no means to price the risk.

The article raises the question of whether Nvidia's advantage rests on resources that outlast any single leader. The author notes that engineers and institutional capabilities remain and that customer commitments and the product roadmap are expected to continue, which suggests valuable capabilities sit within the organisation. A strategy student can test this against the VRIO framework, asking whether those capabilities are rare, hard to imitate and organised for use. The article also reports, without confirming, that many staff reported directly to the chief executive, a point where dependence on one person could undermine the resource base.

From a supply chain viewpoint the article highlights a concentrated and critical input: computing hardware and software that many downstream users depend on. The concern is not physical disruption but the possibility that leadership turmoil delays product decisions, customer agreements or investment, passing costs and delays to users with few alternatives. Students should read this as a resilience question about concentrated sources and how buyers build alternatives. Export restrictions and scrutiny of partnerships, which the author mentions, add a geopolitical risk that sits outside the supplier.

applications.concept: French and Raven's bases of power
applications.theory: French and Raven identified bases of social power: legitimate, reward, coercive, expert and referent, with informational power added later. Referent power arises from followers' identification with and admiration for a leader, while expert power comes from knowledge or skill. Power that rests on admiration is especially hard to challenge, because followers may withhold criticism out of loyalty.
applications.link: Huang's standing as a teacher of character, shown in his advice to students, rests largely on referent and expert power. The author notes that exceptional performance can make challenge harder when directors, employees and investors become dependent on a celebrated leader. The public nature of his message extended that referent power beyond the firm, so when his conduct was admitted it damaged the trust others placed in the company's promises. This maps onto the theory's point that referent power depends on the leader's perceived integrity.
applications.critique: The model describes sources of power but says little about how leaders use power to resist oversight, and it does not separate a leader's influence from the formal authority the board holds to constrain it.
applications.practice: A board applying this theory should identify where the chief executive's influence rests on personal standing rather than formal authority, then make sure legitimate channels such as independent directors and protected reporting can still challenge decisions. Directors should test whether dissent is being suppressed by admiration as much as by fear.

applications.concept: Principal-agent theory
applications.theory: In principal-agent theory, owners (principals) delegate decisions to managers (agents) whose interests may diverge from theirs, and information asymmetry makes the agent's actions hard to observe. Principals design monitoring, incentives and governance to align behaviour, but these measures are costly and imperfect. The theory implies a continuing role for boards, audit and disclosure rules.
applications.link: Shareholders cannot directly observe a chief executive's personal conduct, and the article shows investors reacting only once revelations emerge, with a cited average immediate loss of around 4 per cent. The author argues that boards' dismissal and succession decisions must be understood through misconduct type and firm performance, which points to governance design as the response. The 2025 study cited, comparing 59 personal misconduct events with 324 financial misconduct events, suggests that the agency problem takes different forms. The author's concern about oversight of a celebrated leader is a monitoring failure in which principals rely on the agent's reputation rather than verification.
applications.critique: The model assumes agents act opportunistically for gain, whereas the article suggests personal indiscretion may not be an agency cost in the narrow sense. It also treats principals as shareholders alone, neglecting employees, families and users of infrastructure, whom the author treats as affected parties.
applications.practice: A board should map which misconduct risks affect performance and which affect trust, then set monitoring to match, including conflict-of-interest disclosure, independent investigation and a credible succession plan. Shareholders should press for these as governance requirements rather than wait for losses to appear.

applications.concept: Supply chain risk management and resilience (Christopher and Peck)
applications.theory: Christopher and Peck treat supply chain risk management as the ability of a network to withstand disruption and recover, or move to a more desirable state afterwards. Resilience depends on understanding vulnerabilities, reducing exposure to concentrated or single sources, and building redundancy, flexibility and visibility across the chain.
applications.link: The article identifies a concentrated supply: Nvidia's hardware and software underpin AI research and commercial development worldwide, so leadership turmoil could delay product decisions, customer agreements or investment. The downstream users the author lists, including smaller laboratories and firms with limited alternatives, are the buyers least able to absorb disruption, which is the classic problem of low-redundancy supply. The author also raises geopolitical risk through export restrictions, which sits outside the supplier. Nvidia's statement that operations and commitments will continue is a visibility measure that supports trust.
applications.critique: The theory was developed mainly for operational and physical disruption, whereas this risk arises from governance and reputation, and the article itself describes these channels as plausible rather than demonstrated. The theory also gives no way of estimating how likely governance shocks are, and dual sourcing is hard where few suppliers offer the capability needed.
applications.practice: A buyer relying on the concentrated supplier should map which products depend on it, identify alternative sources or contractual protections, and run a stress test on how it would respond to a delay in supply. A supplier should disclose its continuity plans to customers so they can plan around them.

applications.concept: The resource-based view and VRIO (Barney)
applications.theory: The resource-based view holds that sustained competitive advantage comes from resources and capabilities that are valuable, rare, costly to imitate and organised to be exploited, which the VRIO framework tests in turn. Resources that pass all four tests can support persistent advantage, while those failing one may yield only temporary advantage or parity.
applications.link: The author argues that Nvidia's engineers and institutional capabilities remain after the chief executive's resignation, and that operations and the product roadmap are expected to continue. Under VRIO, this suggests that valuable resources sit in people and processes rather than in one person. However, the article also reports, without confirming, that many staff reported directly to Mr Huang, which would suggest the capability depends on one individual and may be less organised than claimed. Testing the claim means checking whether institutional knowledge is embedded and whether succession planning would protect it.
applications.critique: VRIO is a snapshot test that does not capture how a leader's personal standing can change the value of a resource over time. The article's evidence on continuity is largely the company's own statement, so the analysis cannot confirm that the capabilities are organised independently of the chief executive.
applications.practice: A strategy team should audit which capabilities depend on named individuals, document and spread institutional knowledge, and build succession plans so that the advantage survives a change of leader.

caseStudy.scenario: A leading chipmaker, whose founder and chief executive has publicly preached that greatness comes from character, resigns after admitting a personal relationship with a customer from a politically sensitive market. Investigations are open into allegations involving foreign intelligence, although the board has said it has no reason to believe security or secrets were compromised. The company supplies computing hardware that many firms and research laboratories depend on. Its shareholders, customers and users must now decide how far to rely on it.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate the view that a chief executive's personal misconduct matters only to shareholders, and advise the board on how to protect the wider stakeholders affected.
evidence: A 2018 study cited in the article reports immediate shareholder losses of around 4 per cent after CEO indiscretions, linked to lost customers and joint ventures.
A 2025 study cited compares 59 personal misconduct events with 324 financial misconduct events and argues that boards should respond according to misconduct type and firm performance.

The board said on 8 November that it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised, and the interim chief executive was named when the resignation was announced on 12 November.
The author argues that the company's hardware and software underpin AI research and commercial development worldwide, so disruption would fall on downstream users with few alternatives.
plan: Define the stakeholders affected beyond shareholders, using the triple bottom line (Elkington) to set out economic, social and environmental costs.
Apply principal-agent theory to explain why owners rely on governance because they cannot observe the chief executive's conduct, and why boards should distinguish misconduct types.
Use French and Raven's bases of power to explain why a celebrated leader's referent and expert power makes challenge harder, and so strengthens the case for independent scrutiny.
Assess supply risk for customers using Christopher and Peck's resilience approach, separating plausible transmission channels from demonstrated effects.
Evaluate the evidence critically: separate admitted conduct from unproven allegations and note that historical averages cannot predict this episode's losses.

Recommend succession planning, independent investigation, enforceable conflict disclosure, protected reporting channels and customer resilience planning, ending with a clear recommendation to the board.
pitfalls: Treating the espionage allegations as established, or using the 4 per cent average as a forecast of Nvidia's loss, both overstate what the article supports.
Discussing only share value and ignoring employees, customers and users of the infrastructure, which are the wider costs the question is designed to test.

alsoConsider: Cressey's fraud triangle of pressure, opportunity and rationalisation

exam.question: Critically evaluate the view that a chief executive's personal conduct is a matter only for the board and shareholders, and discuss how boards can reduce the risks such conduct poses to wider stakeholders.
outline: Define the stakeholders affected and distinguish market costs, such as share price falls, from social costs borne by employees, customers and users of shared infrastructure.
Apply principal-agent theory and French and Raven's bases of power to explain why oversight of a celebrated leader is hard to maintain.
Critically evaluate the evidence, separating admitted conduct from allegations and noting the limits of event-study averages, then recommend governance and resilience measures.

articles.title: Every AI Investment Is Two Bets: Does It Work, Who Profits?
articles.takeaway: Every AI investment bundles a technical bet and a value-capture bet. GE's predictive maintenance worked, but its horizontal platform did not capture the value, so managers should ask who keeps the surplus as well as whether the model works.
articles.summary: The article argues that a substantial AI investment contains two separate bets: whether the system performs its technical task, and whether the investing firm, rather than a customer, rival, supplier or platform, captures the value created. The two bets have independent answers and failure modes. GE's industrial software story shows this: its predictive maintenance capability worked, according to the cited survey evidence, but its Predix platform strategy, aimed at selling a horizontal platform to the wider industrial world, failed. The author contrasts this with Rolls-Royce's Power by the Hour model, which sold flying hours and kept the value of better reliability in its own margins. The article presents a fourth option, which is to decline the ecosystem and deploy the capability internally while changing what the firm sells, and sets out four conditions under which that option is available. It extends the argument to professional services and to the wider AI boom, and closes with five questions for managers to answer before committing money.
keyPoints: AI investment decisions bundle two questions: does the technology work, and does the investing firm keep the value it creates?
The two bets have independent evidence, independent failure modes and should have separate abandonment thresholds.
GE's predictive maintenance capability succeeded, while the platform business built on it failed, so the failure lay in value capture rather than technology.
Jacobides' three ecosystem roles (orchestrator, partner, complementor) omit the option of not entering an ecosystem at all, which the article calls the fourth option.

Internal deployment with outcome-based pricing, as Rolls-Royce did, requires four conditions: an installed base, an outcome that is measurable and attributable, capacity to carry the residual risk, and a contract that can be changed.

modules.reading: The article is about where value is captured and how business architecture determines returns, which is central to strategic positioning and business models. GE's choice between building a horizontal platform for new industries and selling outcomes to its existing installed base is a diversification and business model decision. The argument that owned assets only protect returns for a particular route to market is a resource and capability argument. Students should use the piece to connect resources, business model and value capture.

Seen from project management, GE's platform push is a programme that kept accelerating after an external assessment in 2016 found Predix less developed than claimed. The article's separate tests and abandonment thresholds for each bet are a stage-gate and benefits realisation idea. Students should note that the failure was in governance and benefits definition as well as in delivery.

The article treats the two bets as having different risk profiles and argues that asymmetric payoffs justify a bet only where the cost of failure is bounded and a plausible route to winning exists. It also says that funding a long transformation from a cyclical division removes the patience the strategy needs. Students should read this as a capital allocation and decision-under-uncertainty problem, where the funding horizon and the staging of investment matter as much as expected value.

The article's point that outcome-based contracts replace time-based pricing is a pricing and customer value question. The professional services example, where internal AI makes billable hours a poorer signal of work done, shows how a capability can change a firm's pricing logic. Students should note that marketing theory on value-based pricing has to deal with attribution, namely whether the outcome can be credited to the supplier.

applications.concept: Teece's framework for profiting from technological innovation (appropriability and complementary assets)
applications.theory: Innovators do not always capture the profits from their innovations. Who profits depends on how easily the innovation can be imitated, which is its appropriability, and on who controls the complementary assets needed to commercialise it. Firms with those assets tend to gain the rents, and the choice of commercialisation route determines which assets matter.
applications.link: GE developed a predictive maintenance capability that delivered technical benefits, but the value went to parties with complementary assets in the chosen route, such as hyperscalers at the infrastructure layer and domain specialists at the application layer. GE held an installed base, domain knowledge, service relationships and outcome-based aviation contracts, yet its platform route called on assets it did not have, so its existing assets became irrelevant to the returns it sought. Rolls-Royce, by contrast, used its installed base and service contracts, so the same technology improved its own margins directly. The article's point is that complementary assets protect returns only relative to a specific route to market.
applications.critique: Teece's framework is largely static about the route and treats imitability as a property of the innovation, whereas the article suggests route choice is the decisive variable. Its three-layer account of AI returns is asserted rather than measured, and the evidence for the GE case comes largely from one firm and a small set of comparisons.
applications.practice: Before committing funds, a manager should list the complementary assets each candidate route requires and check which of them the firm already controls. Where the required assets are missing, the cost of building them should be priced into the case, or the firm should choose the route that uses its existing assets.

applications.concept: The VRIO framework and the resource-based view (Barney)
applications.theory: A resource sustains competitive advantage only if it is valuable, rare, inimitable and organised so that the firm can exploit it. Failing the last test means that a potentially advantageous resource produces no advantage. The resource-based view treats the firm's internal resources as the source of its advantage.
applications.link: GE's installed base and outcome-based aviation contracts were valuable and hard to replicate, so they pass the first and third tests. The AI capability itself is becoming available to competitors on broadly similar terms, so it fails the rarity test, which the article says means it cannot by itself produce advantage.
